markdownRemark.html:
Every photo editor has an HSL panel. I use it all the time, and a while ago I realized I couldn’t say what the “S” actually measured. I don’t like using a tool I can’t explain, so I asked Claude, and the answer turned out to be shorter than I expected: HSL is not a different way of storing color. It is the same three RGB numbers, relabelled so a human can steer them.

This is part of a series about color that grew out of a loose end in my Exposure vs Brightness article. In What an RGB number actually means I learned that an RGB number is an instruction, not a color, and in Where the horseshoe comes from where the map of visible color comes from. HSL doesn’t live on that map at all, which is why it gets its own article. Here is what I wanted to know:

  • What is HSL, exactly? What does each letter measure?
  • What is HSV, and how is it different? Why do both exist?
  • Where do they go wrong?

The color series: 1. What an RGB number actually means · 2. Where the horseshoe comes from · 3. HSL and HSV: RGB with different knobs (you are here) · 4. Lab: numbers that match what you see · 5. Why gradients go muddy

Disclaimer: This is still learning in public. The arithmetic below I recomputed in code, and I say where a claim comes from Claude and not from me. The history and the “which program uses what” parts I have not checked myself, so if you know better, please tell me in the comments. I’d rather be corrected than be confidently wrong.

You can play with every number in this article. The small widgets do the real math.

Key takeaways:

  • HSL and HSV are RGB with the axes relabelled. They share the same hue and the same “chroma” (the gap between the biggest and smallest channel). They differ only in how they measure the rest.
  • HSL lightness is the average of the biggest and smallest channel. HSV “value” is just the biggest channel. Neither knows anything about how bright a color looks.
  • The word “saturation” means two different things. The dark teal #33505C is 29% saturated in HSL and 45% in HSV.
  • Use them to steer a color, not to judge one. Pure yellow and pure blue have the same lightness in HSL and the same value in HSV.

HSL is RGB with the axes relabelled

Picture the RGB cube: black at one corner, white at the opposite one, the other six corners red, green, blue, yellow, cyan and magenta. Every gray (R = G = B) lies on the diagonal between black and white. Now stand the cube on its black corner so that diagonal points straight up. Seen from the side and from above, it looks like this:

Interactive illustration (rgb-cube). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

HSL is cylindrical coordinates around that upright axis:

  • L (lightness) is how high up the axis you are.
  • S (saturation) is how far out from the axis you are.
  • H (hue) is which direction you are in.

Seen from above, the cube’s outline is a hexagon, not a circle. That one fact explains most of HSL’s quirks.

Here is the arithmetic. Call the biggest channel M, the smallest m, and the gap between them C (chroma, the raw distance from gray). Channels are fractions from 0 to 1.

L = (M + m) / 2

S = C / (1 − |2L − 1|)

I’ll work it with the dark teal from the exposure article, #33505C, which is 51 · 80 · 92. As fractions that is 0.200, 0.314, 0.361. The biggest is M = 0.361 (blue), the smallest is m = 0.200, so C = 0.161.

L = (0.361 + 0.200) / 2 = 28%

S = 0.161 / (1 − |2 × 0.280 − 1|) = 0.161 / 0.561 = 29%

The hue comes out at 198°, just past cyan toward blue. Those are the same 28% and 29% I quoted in the exposure article, now with a reason. Move the sliders and watch every step update:

Interactive illustration (hsl-steps). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

For nerds: how the hue is computed

Claude explained this to me. The hue formula goes back to Alvy Ray Smith’s 1978 paper on HSV.

The largest channel picks one of three 120° sectors: red at 0°, green at 120°, blue at 240°. The other two channels slide you along that sector:

  • If red is biggest: H = 60° × ((G − B) / C mod 6)
  • If green is biggest: H = 60° × ((B − R) / C + 2)
  • If blue is biggest: H = 60° × ((R − G) / C + 4)

For the teal, blue is the biggest, so H = 60 × ((0.200 − 0.314) / 0.161 + 4) = 198°. The secondaries sit halfway between: yellow 60°, cyan 180°, magenta 300°.

This is linear interpolation along the edges of the hexagon, which is why equal steps in degrees are not equal steps to the eye.

HSV: same idea, a different definition

HSV (also called HSB, B for brightness) is HSL’s sibling. Both date from 1978 (according to Wikipedia, HSV is Alvy Ray Smith’s and HSL is Joblove and Greenberg’s). HSV uses the same hue and the same C, and changes the other two:

V = M

S = C / M

That is the whole difference. Value is simply the biggest channel, and saturation is measured against it. For the teal: V = 0.361 = 36% and S = 0.161 / 0.361 = 45%. The same color is 29% saturated in HSL and 45% saturated in HSV.

Where HSL’s shape is a double cone, with black at the bottom, white on top and the pure colors around the middle, HSV’s is a single cone. Black is the tip, and the pure colors and white share the top face. Try a few colors and compare the two answers:

Interactive illustration (hsl-vs-hsv). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Things to notice with the buttons:

  • Pure colors are different heights. Pure red, yellow and blue are L 50% in HSL, but V 100% in HSV.
  • White is different too. In HSL it is L 100%. In HSV it is V 100% with S 0%, the same V as pure red.
  • The pastel #E6B8C8 is S 48% and L 81% in HSL, but S 20% and V 90% in HSV. In HSV it is “mostly bright and a bit colorful”, in HSL it is “very light, moderately colorful”.

I asked Claude why both exist, and this is its answer (I have not checked it): HSV matches how a color picker works, with a square where the top edge is “full strength” for every hue. HSL is symmetric, so “make it lighter” and “make it darker” are equally easy and both reach the same hue. CSS has hsl() but no hsv(), and many color pickers use HSV (Photoshop calls it HSB). I have not checked which one my own editors use, so look at the letters on the sliders.

Three things they get wrong

HSL and HSV date from the late 1970s, when computer graphics researchers wanted a more intuitive way to choose colors than three raw numbers: cheap math and three knobs that feel natural. They were never meant to match how we see. Three examples:

  1. Lightness is not brightness. Pure yellow #FFFF00 and pure blue #0000FF both score S = 100% and L = 50% in HSL, and V = 100% in HSV. Yellow is obviously much brighter.
  2. Saturation near black is misleading. #1A0000 is almost black, yet both models say it is 100% saturated (HSL L is 5%, HSV V is 10%). At that low a level, a tiny amount of red is the most color that exists.
  3. Hue degrees are not perceptually even. It is a hexagon, not a perceptual circle. This is the standard criticism and I didn’t measure it myself.

The widget below shows the first two. Flip the switch to see a measure of perceived lightness (Lab L*, which gets its own article, Lab: numbers that match what you see):

Interactive illustration (hsl-lies). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Pro Tip: Use HSL or HSV to steer a color and nudge things around, but don’t use them to judge how bright two colors are. A yellow and a blue at the same “L” are nowhere near the same brightness.

What I took away

HSL and HSV are RGB wearing a different label. They are handy because “make it a bit lighter” or “make it less colorful” are one slider each, and they are honest about being a rearrangement of the same three numbers. That also means they inherit everything about color spaces: what the numbers mean still depends on the space they are in (What an RGB number actually means).

What they cannot do is tell me how a color looks. Yellow and blue with the same “L” differ hugely in brightness. So I started wondering what an honest lightness would look like, one where the number matches what I see. That is a color system called Lab, and I cover it in Lab: numbers that match what you see.

Did I get something wrong, or do you use these models differently? The comments are open.
